Description: Alexander W. Gofton (CSIRO). Title: Climate change will contract, but not eliminate, the Australian range of the Asian longhorned tick, Haemaphysalis longicornis.

Mapping and transfer. Estimate current climatic suitability across continental Australia and Tasmania from a model calibrated across the native and invaded ranges (transfer in space), and project it to future climates (transfer in time). Outputs inform surveillance and livestock risk management.
Continuous relative climatic suitability (cloglog) and binary suitable/unsuitable maps; ensemble change classes and management categories for future scenarios.
Haemaphysalis longicornis Neumann, 1901 (Acari: Ixodidae). Only the parthenogenetic lineage occurs in Australia; native-range records pool bisexual and parthenogenetic populations.

Calibration: accessible area M (1,000-km buffers around records) in East Asia, eastern North America and Oceania (Australia, New Zealand, south-west Pacific). Projection: continental Australia and Tasmania, excluding Lord Howe and Macquarie Islands and external territories.
Spatial resolution 2.5 arc-minutes (about 4.6 km); extent 112–154°E, 9–44°S for projections. Temporal: 1970–2000 baseline; future periods 2021–2040, 2041–2060, 2061–2080, 2081–2100.
Presence-only occurrence records.
Climatic: bioclimatic variables (temperature, precipitation), Thornthwaite aridity index; candidates also included PET, climatic moisture index and VPD.

Off-host survival and development of ixodid ticks are governed by temperature (development, questing, overwinter survival) and atmospheric moisture balance (desiccation of non-feeding stages). Each candidate predictor set spans thermal regime or limits, temperature variability, moisture supply and desiccation stress.

Climatic niche conserved between native and invaded ranges and through time (tested for space: niche equivalency/similarity); native and Oceanian populations near equilibrium with climate (North American population still spreading); target-group background corrects sampling bias; no evolutionary adaptation within the projection horizon; delta-downscaled mean climate adequately represents future change.

MaxEnt 3.4 (maxent.jar via dismo). Chosen over GLM, GAM, BRT, down-sampled random forest and ensembles because it had the lowest transfer omission and best transfer calibration (Supplementary Methods S1; Table S3). Final model: unweighted consensus of three MaxEnt configurations.

Figure 1: data → region-balanced background → a priori predictor sets × MaxEnt settings → selection by leave-one-region-out and spatial-block CV → consensus + bootstrap → current and future projection → management translation.

R 4.4.1; terra, sf, dismo (MaxEnt 3.4), predicts, ecospat, envirem, tidyverse. Code embedded in code_6, code_7, code_8; outputs in outputs_6–9 and processed_data_6–8; rasters released in outputs_9/rasters (Table S25).
Haemaphysalis longicornis as recorded in GBIF backbone, ALA and source publications; no synonyms merged.
Occurrences (presence of populations at localities).
GBIF; Atlas of Living Australia (download 2026-02-04); Rochlin (2019) compilation for North America and the Pacific; Zhang et al. (2019) for China.
Opportunistic records and published surveys; no designed sampling.
389 records after thinning and stratification: East Asia 215, North America 53, Oceania 121 (Australia 66). 71 known Australian records (training + ALA) used for gap analysis.
Spatially thinned to ≥ 10 km; regionally stratified so no region exceeds 35% of records (random subsampling of East Asian records). One Himalayan record assigned to East Asia.
Records without coordinates and duplicate localities removed.
None.

10,000 points within M, allocated among regions by land area and drawn within regions by a target-group sampling-effort surface (GBIF Ixodidae + Zhang et al. 2019; Gaussian kernel σ = 1°, normalised within region, floor 0.02). Independent 10,000 uniform points for evaluation; uniform background for sensitivity.

Strong regional sampling imbalance (target-group records dominated by North America) corrected by region-normalised bias surface; sensitivity to a uniform background reported (Figure S10). North American records do not represent equilibrium.

Leave-one-region-out (3 folds: East Asia, North America, Oceania) and spatial blocks (5° × 5° blocks, 5 folds). Australian records evaluated separately with the Oceania-withheld model. No external independent dataset.

19 candidates: WorldClim 2.1 BIO1–7, BIO10–17; ENVIREM PET, Thornthwaite aridity index, climatic moisture index; CHELSA v2.1 mean annual VPD. Used in final model: bio1, bio2, bio12, bio13, bio15, bio17, aridity_idx.
Global, 2.5 arc-minutes, WGS 84. CHELSA VPD aggregated from 30″.
WorldClim 2.1 1970–2000; ENVIREM built on an earlier WorldClim baseline; CHELSA 1981–2010.
BIO8, BIO9, BIO18, BIO19 excluded (discontinuities). Baseline mismatch between ENVIREM and WorldClim 2.1 handled by applying future aridity change as an anomaly (S3).

WorldClim 2.1 CMIP6 downscaled monthly Tmin, Tmax, precipitation; GCMs: ACCESS-CM2, ACCESS-ESM1-5, CMCC-ESM2, CNRM-ESM2-1, EC-Earth3-Veg, GISS-E2-1-G, IPSL-CM6A-LR, MIROC6, MPI-ESM1-2-HR, MRI-ESM2-0 (ECS 2–5 K; one per family); SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0, SSP5-8.5; four 20-year periods. Bioclim variables recomputed from monthly data; aridity from Hargreaves PET applied as anomaly.
MESS (univariate) and ExDet NT2 (combinations) for current and every future scenario; clamped vs. unclamped predictions compared (Figure S18, Table S12).
Ten predictor sets defined a priori on physiological grounds (Table S4); set A reproduces stepwise-VIF selection.
All sets |Spearman ρ| ≤ 0.75 and VIF < 5 across M (evaluation background).

Features L, LQ, LQH, LQHP × β = 0.5–8 tuned per set; threshold features off; clamping on; cloglog output; 10,000 background points. Selected members: set H (bio1, bio12, bio15, aridity_idx; LQ, β = 3); set C (bio1, bio2, bio12, bio15, aridity_idx; LQ, β = 2); set G (bio1, bio2, bio13, bio17, aridity_idx; LQH, β = 4); non-zero features 6, 8, 29.
Sequential: omission filter (mean LORO OR10 ≤ 0.30 and block OR10 ≤ 0.20), then lowest rank sum of LORO and block AUC and CBI.
Unweighted mean cloglog of the three top predictor-set configurations (consensus); evaluated with all members refitted in each fold.
MaxEnt permutation importance per member; consensus marginal response curves with 95% bootstrap intervals (Figure 3).
10-km thinning; spatially structured cross-validation (region and block).
10th-percentile training presence of the consensus (cloglog = 0.400); maximum sensitivity + specificity (0.463) as sensitivity analysis (Table S6).
AUC, continuous Boyce index, OR10. Mean LORO AUC 0.86, CBI 0.81, OR10 0.27; block AUC 0.82, CBI 0.84, OR10 0.18; Australia with Oceania withheld AUC 0.94, OR10 0.47 (Table 1, Table S5).

Response curves consistent with tick physiology; global projection reproduces native and North American ranges (Figure S6); niche equivalency/similarity tests (Table S7); agreement with an independent process-based life-cycle model built from laboratory parameters (Figure 9, Table S18).

Continuous cloglog suitability and binary maps (current); per-GCM binary maps summarised as ensemble median, GCM agreement, change classes and management categories (future). Areas from true cell areas.
Single algorithm; predictor-set uncertainty propagated through the three-member consensus; algorithm comparison reported (Table S3).
30 bootstrap resamples of presences within regions (Figure S8); background sensitivity (Figure S10); threshold sensitivity (Table S6).
10 GCMs × 4 SSPs × 4 periods; ANOVA partitioning among SSP, GCM and SDM bootstrap (Table S13); alternative GCM ensembles (Table S15); results also expressed at global warming levels (Table 4).
MESS, ExDet NT2 and clamping effects mapped; suitable area reported with and without novel climate (Table S12).
